title: If a parent class is `Serializable`, how do you restrict serialization of the child class (throw `NotSerializableException` in `writeObject`/`readObject`)?
shortTitle: How do you prevent a child class from being serialized?

s1_definition.profdef: Serializability is inherited, so if a parent class implements Serializable, every subclass is automatically serializable even though the subclass does not declare the interface itself, and you cannot un-implement an interface. To forbid serialization of a specific subclass, you override the private writeObject and readObject methods in that subclass and have them throw NotSerializableException, which makes any attempt to serialize or deserialize an instance of that subclass fail loudly while leaving the parent and other subclasses serializable.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, suppose the general Account form is approved for mailing, which is like the parent being Serializable. A special VaultAccount is a kind of Account, so it automatically inherits that mailing approval. But the bank decides vault accounts are too sensitive to ever be mailed. Since you cannot peel the inherited approval off a subclass, the vault account instead stamps a hard rule on its own packet: if anyone tries to seal or open this packet, immediately refuse and raise an alarm. That hard refusal is throwing NotSerializableException from writeObject and readObject.
s1_definition.oneliner: Serializability is inherited and cannot be removed, so to block a subclass you override writeObject and readObject to throw NotSerializableException, failing any serialize or deserialize attempt on that subclass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Serializability is inherited, so if a parent class implements Serializable, every subclass is automatically serializable even though the subclass does not declare the interface itself, and you cannot un-implement an interface. To forbid serialization of a specific subclass, you override the private writeObject and readObject methods in that subclass and have them throw NotSerializableException, which makes any attempt to serialize or deserialize an instance of that subclass fail loudly while leaving the parent and other subclasses serializable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, suppose the general Account form is approved for mailing, which is like the parent being Serializable. A special VaultAccount is a kind of Account, so it automatically inherits that mailing approval. But the bank decides vault accounts are too sensitive to ever be mailed. Since you cannot peel the inherited approval off a subclass, the vault account instead stamps a hard rule on its own packet: if anyone tries to seal or open this packet, immediately refuse and raise an alarm. That hard refusal is throwing NotSerializableException from writeObject and readObject.

**One line to remember:** Serializability is inherited and cannot be removed, so to block a subclass you override writeObject and readObject to throw NotSerializableException, failing any serialize or deserialize attempt on that subclass.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The general Account class is Serializable so ordinary accounts can be cached. A VaultAccount extends Account and therefore inherits serializability, but the bank forbids vault accounts from ever being serialized. This is exactly the inherited-serializability problem.

Problem 2 — Because you cannot un-implement Serializable, the VaultAccount throws NotSerializableException from writeObject and readObject, so any serialize or deserialize of a vault account fails while ordinary accounts still serialize fine. This is exactly the override-and-throw solution.

The code defines a Serializable `Account`, a `VaultAccount` subclass that blocks serialization, and a `RestrictSubclassDemo` main class that serializes an ordinary account successfully and shows the vault account being rejected.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
restrict-subclass-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/core/
│       ├── Account.java               (parent, Serializable)
│       ├── VaultAccount.java           (child, blocks serialization)
│       └── RestrictSubclassDemo.java   (main)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/*.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.core.RestrictSubclassDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are an ordinary Account for SAV2001 with balance 1000000.00 and a VaultAccount for VLT9001 with balance 50000000.00 and vaultId VAULT-A.

Step 1: The demo serializes the ordinary account. Because Account implements Serializable and defines no blocking hook, the engine writes the fields and produces a byte array successfully.

Step 2: The demo attempts to serialize the vault account. The engine finds the vault account's private writeObject method and invokes it.

Step 3: That writeObject method immediately throws NotSerializableException naming VaultAccount, so no bytes are produced and the operation fails.

Step 4: The demo catches that exception and logs it as a correct rejection, confirming the restriction holds even though the subclass inherited serializability from its parent.

Step 5: The symmetric readObject override guarantees that even if vault-account bytes existed, reading them back would also throw, so the block is complete in both directions.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Ordinary Account serialized OK, bytes = 200
Oct 30, 2026 ... SEVERE: VaultAccount serialization correctly rejected
java.io.NotSerializableException: com.bank.core.VaultAccount
	at com.bank.core.VaultAccount.writeObject(...)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  serialize(obj)
    │
    ├─ obj = Account(SAV2001)                 ├─ obj = VaultAccount(VLT9001)
    │  Serializable, no block hook            │  inherits Serializable
    │  writeObject default                    │  writeObject OVERRIDDEN
    │  → fields written                       │  → throw NotSerializableException
    ▼                                         ▼
  byte[200] produced                     FAIL (no bytes) — named VaultAccount
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Block Subclass Serialization ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  L: VaultAccount IS-A Account but narrows one behavior    │
  │     (serialization) by design, failing fast and loudly   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account             │ implements Serializable
  │  # accountId: String          │
  │  # balance: BigDecimal        │
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ extends (inherits Serializable)
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        VaultAccount           │
  │  - vaultId: String            │
  │  + writeObject(out)  → THROW  │ NotSerializableException
  │  + readObject(in)    → THROW  │ NotSerializableException
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for VaultAccount serialization:
    Pre:  none
    Post: ALWAYS throws NotSerializableException (both directions)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. serialize(Account)       → default writeObject → byte[200]
  2. serialize(VaultAccount)  → VaultAccount.writeObject() → THROW
  3. catch NotSerializableException → logged as correct rejection
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Serializability is inherited, and that is the key fact. If a parent class implements Serializable, every subclass is automatically serializable too, even though the subclass never declares the interface, and there is no way in Java to un-implement an interface on a subclass. So I cannot remove serializability through the type system; I have to enforce the restriction through behavior.

The way to do that is to override the special serialization hook methods in the subclass. The engine calls a private writeObject method during serialization and a private readObject method during deserialization. By defining both in the subclass and having each throw a NotSerializableException that names the class, I make any attempt to serialize or deserialize an instance of that subclass fail loudly, while the parent and all other subclasses stay fully serializable.

I always override both directions deliberately. Overriding only writeObject stops the bytes from being created, but if bytes existed somehow, readObject would still try to read them, so blocking both guarantees the subclass can never be flattened or rebuilt. In a bank this is a real security pattern: an ordinary Account is cacheable, but a VaultAccount or an internal settlement account must never be flattened to bytes that could be cached, logged, or transmitted, so it hard-fails serialization even though its convenient parent is serializable.

I also prefer this over trying to mark every field transient, because a future developer could add a new non-transient field and quietly reopen the hole, whereas throwing from writeObject and readObject blocks the whole operation no matter what fields exist. So my complete answer is that because serializability is inherited and cannot be removed, I restrict a subclass by overriding writeObject and readObject to throw NotSerializableException in both directions, which is a clean, field-independent, security-correct block.

---

keyPoints: Child inherits Serializable from parent — must actively block it
Alternative: custom readObjectNoData() to reject deserialization
Design consideration: make parent non-serializable if children should not be
